Hey guys!
I know that Amazon Affiliate sites aren't always considered beermoney, but this was a popular post on Reddit and I think people here could find it useful also.

P.S.- This will be me sharing my experiences with Amazon so far. I am by no means a guru, and I still have a ton to learn. However I wanted to show you that you don't have to be an expert to make money.

P.P.S.- Amazon does not accept affiliates from Arkansas, Colorado, Maine, Missouri, Rhode Island, or Vermont.

P.P.P.S.- Amazon does accept affiliates from other countries into it's Amazon.com program, but it also has country specific programs such as amazon.uk and others. In some cases it's more profitable to create an Amazon Affiliate site in your language rather than try to compete with numerous Amazon.com affiliates.

My history with Amazon

I found out about Amazon Affiliate sites almost a year ago, but I never thought about creating my own.

Last August I read a couple of long Amazon Affiliate journeys on BHW and that spurred my interest in creating a website even though it wasn't Amazon Affiliate focused at first.

Then last December I stumbled upon another Amazon Affiliate thread, and I decided that this was something I was interested in doing myself.

My first site is the one that I talk about in my blog post which is what this post is based on.

After seeing that I enjoy the process of creating the sites and writing content for them I created 2 more sites, and I have ideas for numerous other ones which I will work on this summer.

2 of my sites are still in the baby stages so I haven't made a lot from them, but I've made a total of around $50 from this site even though my timing for creating it was absolutely horrible. (More on this later)

What you should know before starting

  • This takes a lot of work and you will not see the reward for at least 2 months. (If not more)
  • It is possible that your site will not earn you any money at all. *(I haven't had this happen to me yet as even my "baby" sites had at least one sale on them.)
  • This is more of a long-term strategy where you invest a lot of time now and reap the rewards later. (With investing an hour or so every month checking your site and adding a new post)
  • You have to do keyword research! (You will not succeed otherwise)
  • If you don't enjoy any of the aspects of creating a website or writing content for it, don't do this. It's not worth it.
  • Wordpress is better than Blogger especially if you plan on making your site fairly big. (Blogger is still usable, but WordPress.org trumps it in almost every way)

Starting out

I bought my domain from GoDaddy for $4, (With privacy protection), and I hosted my website on Blogger which in hindsight was the wrong decision as my second blog was hosted on Wordpress and it is so much better...

I used Market Samurai for keyword research and they have a 7 day free trial. ref non-ref

Researching your niche

These rules are what I went by when doing niche and keyword research, but you can look around the Internet and see what others are doing or add your own twist to it.

I want my niche to:

  • Have some fairly expensive products. $100+
  • Have some lower priced products.
  • Have many products on Amazon.
  • Have fairly low competition.
  • Be something I'm fairly interested in writing about.
  • And be something that people might research online.

The top 10 Google results for my niche should:

  • Not have an exact match domain for my niche. (If my keyword is best calculators, I don't want a website called bestcalculators.com to be in the top 10 of Google already)
  • Have less than 10 backlinks to the page the content related to my keyword is on.
  • Have few .edu or .gov backlinks.
  • Not have a high Trust flow.
  • Not have exact match titles, descriptions, or headers.

I use Market Samurai for my keyword research, and you can follow along here if that's what you're also using.

Some general guidelines I set for myself:

  • The main keyword should at least get 300 searches per month.
  • The more long tails I can think of off the top of my head, and the more good long tails Market Samurai gives me the better. (Long tail keywords are specific keywords that are usually easier to rank for. Ex: "Best track spikes for the 400 meter dash", "most reliable desk lamp under 50 dollars", etc... They will not have a high number of searches per month, but they're very valuable.
  • Use buyer oriented keywords. If a person searches "track spikes" or "track" they might not be looking to buy anything, but if a person searches for a specific item or uses search terms like "best track spikes under $50", "cheapest hard drive to buy today", "cheap replacement for blahblahblah product" etc...

SEO and site creation

You can purchase a 99 cent domain from GoDaddy and NameCheap has deals from time to time also, and I decided not to go through the basics of setting up a website and connecting a domain in either of my posts, but if this is something people are interested in I could make a couple of tutorials for Blogger/Wordpress.org. Or just use Google!

If you did proper keyword research it shouldn't be too hard to rank for your keywords, but here are some SEO basics:

  • Make sure that your content is actually good!
  • Use custom permalinks (if on Blogger) and SEO plugins (if on Wordpress)
  • Create custom search descriptions to draw people in.
  • Use Categories, Labels, or Tags to make sorting through your content easier for you and your visitors.
  • Use your keyword in the title (if it makes sense), and use phrases/words related to your keyword in your writing.
  • Add your website to Google Webmasters Tools
  • Create a Facebook/Google Plus page and post on it every time a new post/page goes up on your site.
  • Later on you can create a couple of Web 2.0s or comment on niche related blogs for backlinks, but my sites ranked without me doing that. (I'll probably do it this summer to push my rankings into the top 3 though.)
  • Think long term and not short term! Even if the money doesn't come in right away, don't mess it all up by buying links from Fiverr or other sites.
  • To go along with the previous point. DO NOT BUY LINKS!
  • Use tracking software to track your rankings in the serps. You don't have to pay as there are plenty of free websites out there that do it for you.

My results

I've made around $50 from this site which might not seem like a lot for the amount of time I put into the website. (12-16 hours) It comes out to $3.125-$4.16 an hour, but the website will earn more and more as time goes on, and I will need to do less and less work with it.

A quick update 4 months after the original post. I'm making around $50 a month from this site without any work and it's not even the right season for the site. I'm excited for next March/April!

FAQ and other info

Should I use Blogger or Wordpress to create my site?

  • Definitely WordPress if you have the money for hosting. Blogger isn't a terrible free way to start though, so if you can only spare 99 cents for a domain, Blogger is the better option!

Can I become an affiliate if I don't live in the US?

  • You can become an Amazon.com affiliate no matter where you live, unless you live in one of the banned states. (Arkansas, Colorado, Maine, Missouri, Rhode Island, Vermont) You can also join their affiliate program that's specific to your country as there is usually less competition and it would be easier to rank!

Is there anything I must do that shows that I'm an affiliate?

  • You must put this in the footer of your site or your privacy policy: “[Insert your name] is a participant in the Amazon Services LLC Associates Program, an affiliate advertising program designed to provide a means for sites to earn advertising fees by advertising and linking to [insert the applicable site name (amazon.com, amazonsupply.com, or myhabit.com)].”

Is it hard to get into the program?

  • For Amazon.com everyone gets accepted, and then once you get your first sale your site/information undergoes manual review. If you have a fairly high quality site that doesn't break the Amazon Affiliate TOS you should get accepted.

What hosting provider do you use for Wordpress?

  • I use Bluehost. ref non-ref

What are evergreen niches?

  • They are niches that have products that sell fairly evenly throughout the year.

What are seasonal niches?

  • They are niches that sell most of their products during a specific period. (Some products can still sell outside of the season, but the majority of your sales will be in a specific time period.)

How can I find a good niche?

  • Think of products you might research online before buying or just go to Amazon and start browsing through the top 100 products for each category. You can also look for old sites that haven't been updated in forever that have the Amazon disclaimer in the footer and create a site in a similar niche. You might not outrank them right away, but if the products changed and their site hasn't been updated in a year or more you should be able to outrank them or at least get close to them.

If you have other questions ask them in the comments and if I know the answer I'll answer it, and if I don't I'll try to point you in the direction of where you might find it.

Thanks for reading!

This wouldn't work on my Laptop's UEFI - The hardware checks the checksum of the UEFI Loader, and the UEFI Loader checks the actual UEFI. Any break and the Laptop doesn't boot any more.
So if I switch back to legacy bios will it completely disable UEFI/nullify this exploit?

No, the CSM "Compatibility Support Module" on modern boards is only a shim that loaded into UEFI. It doesn't replace the UEFI, it only emulates the original BIOS. There would be few boards, if any, that have both a UEFI and original working BIOS wrote for them.

Luckily most modern boards are shipped with an easier to replace, 8 pin chip for the BIOS. Removing a small chip is easier and devices to verify or write to the chip are simpler.
Okay, thank you for explaining that. Is this chip typically soldered onto the board/ easy to replace ? For a little more background I'm using a MSI mobo in a custom desktop.

Sometimes it's soldered, sometimes it's put in a socket. Regardless, it's easier than 28 to 40 pin chips of old. If it is soldered, I've reflashed bricked BIOSs with just jumper cables, hooked up to the 5 to 6 pins required to access the chip. It's it's socketed, it's easy to pull.

Either way, there are much simpler devices for serial flash. Flashrom.org supports a half dozen home-made and $20 adapters, much cheaper than any universal programmer ($200 and up).
